chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Learning another man's solos without imitating him
summary: McRae learned the Joe Thomas feature but played around it, a method he also used with Hawkins patterns.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Because we had a lot to contend with, you know. So I'm down with (inaudible), you know, Jimmy Crawford -- the drummer's betting Jimmy that I wouldn't play the book.
They had a set set up for me. "If he get through this, we'll test him out," you know. So after I -- went out to the ballroom that night, they put this hard set to stop me with.
But they didn't know I had went and got the records and familiarize myself. I had worked on the records for two days in New York.
Even Joe Thomas' 'Let's Keep Smiling' which was a smash hit (inaudible). So I figured, well

I got to learn this thing and sing it too. In fact, I learned the solo not for myself. I just wanted to familiarize myself so when I play Thomas' solos, I could play as much of it as I wanted, but it would be me plahing, you know, instead of just playing note-for-note what he play.

I never did believe in that. If I was gonna come and play in your place for a month or so, I would learn -- I would familiarize myself with the (inaudible) you play, you know, what you had to do in that particular chair and your solos.
But I would learn it, but I wouldn't learn them to the point where I would just, you know, imitate you.
I would learn to play around to make it sound almost like you, you know. And that's one of the things that Coleman found out that what I was doing.
I wasn't playing strictly Coleman Hawkins, I would take some of his patterns and work around it, you know.
Just run through some of -- you know,
